dek: Keep the records that explain an agent’s actions, then check them against what was allowed. Today’s stories cover readable session history, tool-level evaluation, evidence coverage in AI log analysis, and two fixes for trustworthy trace delivery.

stories.title: Mainplane keeps agent session state in readable files on a separate server
stories.summary: The developer’s first-party launch describes append-only session files that serve as both agent state and execution traces, while tools run on connected machines.
body: Mainplane is an agent harness: software that coordinates model calls, tools and session state. In its first-party Show HN launch, developer Alexander describes keeping that coordination on a separate server while shell and file operations run on connected worker machines. Each session is stored in one append-only file, where new events are added at the end rather than rewriting earlier ones, which the developer presents as both recoverable state and an agent trace.

For illustration, an engineer investigating a failed task could inspect the session file on the server even if the laptop running a tool had disconnected. The design separates where actions happen from where their history lives. The announcement says a new session can search an earlier state file for context, rather than relying on a condensed summary. That is a described workflow, not an independently tested recovery guarantee.

The server holds model credentials and routes tool calls over a built-in private network that uses WireGuard, an encrypted VPN protocol. The developer also explicitly describes unrestricted agent access within the chosen worker computer. Readable session files therefore help investigation but do not establish permission enforcement, complete audit coverage or safe execution. This edition has not tested the harness.
stories.takeaway: For teams evaluating workstation agents: inspect session-file coverage and recovery behavior, and assess worker permissions separately from trace readability.

stories.title: Arize’s tool-call checks catch leaks that an answer-only judge misses
stories.summary: In a synthetic support-agent experiment, checking tool calls exposed unauthorized customer lookups that a model judging only final answers often missed.
body: Arize Phoenix records the steps an AI agent takes so engineers can inspect and evaluate its behavior. Arize’s new experiment uses those traces to investigate indirect prompt injection: instructions in an external page that redirect an agent away from the user’s task. A support agent read 100 poisoned order pages, once each, using synthetic customer records.

Arize reports 28 unauthorized lookups that returned data. A deterministic check examined tool calls against the logged-in customer’s permitted scope and flagged all 28. A language-model judge reading only final answers identified five. The difference matters because an agent can retrieve forbidden information without repeating it in its reply. In the article’s example, an order-summary request led to lookups for a different customer named by the fetched page.

The team then bound customer tools to the session identity in code. In that test, 20 attempted out-of-scope lookups returned no data. These are vendor-reported results from one experimental setup, not a universal security rate. Arize also describes applying evaluations and monitors to production traces. Engineers should validate a judge against known tool-level outcomes before treating its score as evidence of access compliance.
stories.takeaway: For teams evaluating agents with customer-data tools: test access scope at the tool boundary and compare answer judges with trace-level ground truth.

stories.title: Elastic checks what log sampling leaves out before generating detection rules
stories.summary: Elastic explains an inspectable extraction loop that builds evidence about a log source before a language model generates detection queries.
body: Elastic Significant Events uses language models to help turn unfamiliar logs into detection rules. Its October 26 engineering article separates learning what a log source contains from generating queries about it. That separation makes it possible to investigate whether a poor rule came from missing evidence or from misusing a fact already extracted.

The extraction stage records Knowledge Indicators: descriptions of services, dependencies, technologies, infrastructure and schema, with supporting log evidence. By default, a run reads up to five batches of 20 documents and can stop earlier when successive batches add nothing new. Code steers sampling toward unexplained entities and diverse message patterns, alongside random samples. A workflow exposes each extraction run for inspection.

In the source’s demonstration, a generic error-level query missed an incident because the relevant services did not record severity in the expected way. The example shows why checking generated query syntax alone cannot establish detection coverage. Engineers building AI-assisted operations tools should inspect what the model actually saw. This is the first part of a vendor engineering series; query generation and final event detection are reserved for later articles, and extraction can still miss important facts.
stories.takeaway: For teams building AI log-analysis workflows: evaluate evidence coverage separately from generated-query quality, and retain inspectable extraction runs.

stories.title: Langfuse gives telemetry time to flush after gateway connections drain
stories.summary: The gateway now starts a separate telemetry-flush deadline after connections finish draining, preventing slow streams from consuming both budgets.
body: Langfuse is a platform for recording and evaluating AI application activity. Its AI gateway handles model requests and sends telemetry about them. Release v4.70.1 fixes a shutdown problem: a slow connection could consume the entire shutdown deadline, leaving no time to send pending inference records or operational metrics.

The linked implementation separates connection draining from telemetry flushing. Draining gives existing connections time to finish after a termination signal. The flush clock now starts after that phase ends. For illustration, a long-running streamed answer could reach the connection-drain limit during a deployment; pending telemetry would then receive its own opportunity to leave the process. This describes the intended mechanism, not a guarantee against every source of lost records.

Both timeouts default to ten seconds and accept values from one to 300 seconds. The previous shutdown setting remains a fallback for connection draining, with a deprecation warning. Kubernetes operators must allow enough termination grace for any pre-stop delay and both budgets. The release also renews expired media URLs when previews reopen; that is separate from the telemetry-delivery fix.
stories.takeaway: For self-hosted gateway operators: review termination grace periods and test record delivery during deployments after upgrading.

stories.title: Braintrust batches log uploads and records the tool output the model saw
stories.summary: The JavaScript SDK adds delayed batching in long-lived Node processes and fixes tool-output records and duplicate token accounting.
body: Braintrust’s JavaScript SDK records AI application activity for debugging and evaluation. Version 3.40.0 changes both how those records are delivered and what some contain. In long-lived Node processes, nearby log rows are now combined into fewer HTTP requests, with a delay of up to one second before flushing by default.

The release tells applications to call flush() before shutting down on signals or through process.exit(). BRAINTRUST_FLUSH_DELAY_MS controls the delay; serverless and other runtimes continue to flush immediately by default. For illustration, an application that logs a final tool call and exits immediately should explicitly finish sending its records rather than assume the batching timer has already fired.

The SDK also changes records for AI SDK tools that define toModelOutput: tool spans, which record individual operations, and parent tool results capture the transformed value shown to the model instead of the raw execution result. Pi coding-agent fixes preserve system instructions and tool declarations, and keep token usage on child model-call spans to avoid counting it again on the parent task. These are release-note claims; teams should check their own trace contents and shutdown behavior after upgrading.
stories.takeaway: For JavaScript instrumentation owners: await final delivery at shutdown and verify that tool outputs and token totals match the model calls you intended to record.
